h1: Tomato and ketchup notes in old hoppy beer explained
title: Tomato and Ketchup Notes in Old IPA | Craft Beer School
desc: Why an old IPA starts to smell of tomato leaf or ketchup, the hop oxidation and warm storage behind it and how breweries slow it down.
teaser: When a hazy IPA starts tasting like a ketchup sachet, the hops did not change their mind. Oxygen and heat changed them.
standfirst: Tomato leaf and ketchup notes are among the most recognisable signs of an old, oxidised hoppy beer. They arrive as fresh hop aroma fades and they get there faster in the heat. This guide covers what is going on and the packaging and cold chain numbers that hold it back.
sections:
Tasters describe two related notes. Tomato leaf or tomato vine is green, sharp and slightly catty, like brushing past tomato plants in a garden. Ketchup is sweeter, cooked and savoury, with a vinegary, spiced edge. In an ageing IPA they often appear together, usually alongside fading fruit, a sweet honeyed malt note and a dull, muddy bitterness.

These are not fresh hop aromas. Brewers rarely see them in a beer straight out of the tank. They develop in the package over weeks or months, faster when the beer is warm and when it picked up oxygen at packaging.
Where they sit on the flavour wheel

The standard beer flavour wheel lists catty, with tomato leaf and blackcurrant leaf as reference descriptors, among the stale flavours alongside papery and leathery. That placement tells you something: tomato leaf in an old beer is a staling note, not a hop variety note. Our guide to catty notes in hoppy beer explains how the same family of aromas can come from fresh hops or from age.

The ketchup descriptor is newer and comes largely from drinkers and brewers tasting old hazy and dry-hopped beers. The exact compounds behind it are less well pinned down in published research than the classic staling aldehydes. What is well established is the pattern: heavily hopped beers, oxygen, heat and time.
Why hoppy beers age this way

Dry-hopped beers carry large amounts of hop oil, polyphenols and plant material. Hop oil compounds such as myrcene oxidise readily. Thiols and terpene alcohols that give fresh tropical and citrus character fade or transform. Hop material also brings in oxygen during dry hopping and can carry trace metals that speed oxidation. As the bright fruit disappears, the green, cooked and savoury notes that remain become noticeable.

Heat drives every one of these reactions. A widely used rule of thumb in brewing is that staling roughly doubles for every 10 °C rise in temperature. A hazy IPA stored at 30 °C for a month is effectively much older than one kept at 4 °C for the same month.
The numbers that slow it down

Breweries that keep hoppy beer fresh focus on a few measurable points:

  • Total package oxygen. Many craft brewers aim for dissolved oxygen in packaged hoppy beer below about 50 parts per billion. Every step above that shortens shelf life.
  • Dry hop oxygen pickup. Purging hops with carbon dioxide before adding them and dry hopping during active fermentation, when yeast can scavenge oxygen, both help. Our guide to oxidation in dry-hopped beer after packaging covers the detail.
  • Cold storage. Keeping packaged hoppy beer at 0 to 4 °C from brewery to shop.
  • Short shelf life. Many brewers set shorter best before dates for hazy IPAs than for lagers and print canning dates.

In India, the weak link is usually after the beer leaves the brewery. Unrefrigerated trucks, warehouses that reach well over 35 °C in summer and shop fridges switched off at night can age a hazy IPA in weeks. A brewery can package at an excellent oxygen level and still see ketchup notes in market samples because of what happened in distribution.

Market sampling is the tool. Buy your own beer back from shops in different cities at different ages and taste it against a cold-stored reference from the same batch. If the market samples show tomato and ketchup while the reference is clean, the problem is the chain, not the brewhouse. That evidence is also useful when talking to distributors and retailers about cold storage.
Forced ageing as an early warning

Waiting months to see how a beer ages is slow. Many breweries use forced ageing tests: hold packaged samples warm, often around 30 °C, for a set number of days, then taste them against cold-stored controls. It is not a perfect model of real ageing, but it shows quickly which batches and which packaging runs develop tomato and ketchup notes first.

Your first step: put two cans from your next hoppy batch aside, one cold and one at around 30 °C. Taste them side by side after two weeks. Note whether tomato or ketchup appears and log it with that batch's packaged oxygen reading.
faqs: Why does my old IPA taste like ketchup?
Hop compounds oxidise and fade with time, oxygen and heat, leaving green, cooked and savoury notes such as tomato leaf and ketchup.
Is tomato leaf aroma a hop variety note?
In a fresh beer it can come from certain hops. In an old beer it is usually a staling note, listed with catty on the flavour wheel.
How do breweries keep hoppy beer fresh?
Low package oxygen, careful dry hopping, cold storage from brewery to shop and short best before dates.
How can I test how a beer will age?
Use forced ageing: hold packaged samples warm for a set time and taste them against cold-stored controls.
